comments.text:
1. don't use int-id as the session id for your user, use something else.
not UUID, just any unique identification, can often use the time of last login with username to make it, because user is a database key, it should be easy to track from there, if you want additional optimisations you can add some other identifier to avoid looking up through the whole database.
2. collisions?
auto-increment WITH server-ID. still able to be stored as a single number(append the server ID either at the start or end of the number).
a dedicated central service ONLY for the auto-increment ID can also cover it, unless you are literally creating hundreds of new IDs per second and can't have a task wait on a deferred value.
with correct configuration auto-increment with server-ID can also be set to separate IDs by the creating server which avoids page splits completely.

but UUID v7 is a good choice too. just a bit expensive.

comments.text: I've written my own ID generation for a database once since neither autoincrement nor UUID suited my needs. My needs, specifically, were to allow a bitwise flag to show which shard of the database to query, since different shards contained different parts of the data and it was not guaranteed to be replicated across all shards, and the second was that I needed to be able to include a type and version identifier in the ID itself so I always knew how to handle the object representation even if the database access is asynchronous and still awaiting the actual data to return. It was worth the effort in the end because it solved several problems without adding more bloat to the actual stored data, but it took quite a bit of time to get it right.

comments.text: 1:47 - This is not true, distributed databases do not need central lock to avoid auto-increments collision. You solve this issue with increment and offset combination. For example in MySQL set auto_increment_increment to 10 on both servers and auto_increment_offset to 1 on first and to 2 on second server. First server wil generate 1, 11, 21, 31, ... while second will generate 2, 12, 22, 32, ... They will never colide and you can even move data between them. No need for UUIDs.

comments.text: Nice video, however i would argue using autoincrement ids and exposing them to the client is not a security vulnerability. At best its a security risk, as the attacker can only really utilize it if you have insecure endpoints. This would be the same as security by obscurity. Just by hiding the ids you do not make your application more secure by default, it can serve as an additional protective layer as you would need some sort of leak for the attacker to retrieve the ids. But if you have any database breach or any other source of leak, the insecure endpoints would still be insecure and you have not gotten any security benefit from uuids.
